reminder: The commutator subgroup of a [group](c:group) is the smallest [subgroup](c:subgroup) that contains all [commutators](c:group-commutator) $g^{-1}h^{-1}gh$.
definition: For a [group](c:group) $G$, the commutator subgroup $[G,G]$ is the [subgroup](c:subgroup) generated by all [commutators](c:group-commutator) $[g,h]=g^{-1}h^{-1}gh$ with $g,h\in G$. It is the smallest subgroup of $G$ that contains every commutator, and it is a [normal subgroup](c:normal-subgroup). The quotient $G/[G,G]$ is abelian, and $G$ is abelian exactly when $[G,G]$ is trivial.
examples: In the symmetric group $S_3$, the commutator subgroup is the alternating group $A_3$ of order 3.
In an [abelian group](c:abelian-group), every commutator is the identity, so $[G,G]$ is trivial.
Non-example: the set of single commutators is in general not closed under products, so it is not the commutator subgroup; one must take the subgroup that it generates.

steps: Take a commutator $[g,h]$ and any element $x$ of $G$.
Conjugating gives $x[g,h]x^{-1}=[xgx^{-1},xhx^{-1}]$, which is again a [commutator](c:group-commutator).
So conjugation by $x$ maps the generators of $[G,G]$ into $[G,G]$, and hence maps $[G,G]$ into itself.
Therefore $[G,G]$ is a [normal subgroup](c:normal-subgroup) of $G$.
links.why: It shows that the quotient $G/[G,G]$ always exists, and it is the largest abelian quotient of $G$.

reminder: A comodule over a [comonoid](c:comonoid) $C$ is an object $M$ with a coassociative, counital coaction $M\to M\otimes C$.
definition: Let $C$ be a [comonoid](c:comonoid) with comultiplication $\Delta$ and counit $\varepsilon$ in a monoidal category. A right comodule is an object $M$ with a coaction $\rho:M\to M\otimes C$ such that $(\rho\otimes\mathrm{id})\circ\rho=(\mathrm{id}\otimes\Delta)\circ\rho$ and $(\mathrm{id}\otimes\varepsilon)\circ\rho=\mathrm{id}$. This is the dual of a [module](c:module) over a [monoid](c:monoid), with all arrows reversed.
examples: Every comonoid $C$ is a comodule over itself, with the comultiplication $\Delta$ as coaction.
Let $k[X]$ be the [coalgebra](c:coalgebra) with basis $X$ and $\Delta(x)=x\otimes x$. A vector space graded by $X$ is a comodule over $k[X]$: a vector $v$ of degree $x$ has coaction $v\otimes x$.
Non-example: on $M=k$ over $k[X]$, the map $\rho(1)=1\otimes(x+y)$ with $x\ne y$ is not a coaction, because $\Delta(x+y)=x\otimes x+y\otimes y$ differs from $(x+y)\otimes(x+y)$.

reminder: A [statistic](c:statistic) is complete when no function of it that is not almost surely zero has [expected value](c:expected-value) zero for every parameter.
definition: Let $T$ be a [statistic](c:statistic) of a sample whose [probability distribution](c:probability-distribution) $P_\theta$ depends on a parameter $\theta$. The statistic $T$ is complete when every [measurable function](c:measurable-function) $g$ with $\mathbb{E}_\theta[g(T)]=0$ for all $\theta$ satisfies $g(T)=0$ with probability 1 under every $P_\theta$. In words, the family of laws of $T$ has no nonzero unbiased estimator of zero.
examples: For $n$ independent Bernoulli($p$) samples with $p\in(0,1)$, the sum $T=\sum X_i$ is complete.
For independent samples from $N(\mu,1)$ with unknown $\mu$, the sample mean is complete.
Non-example: for two samples $X_1,X_2$ from $N(\mu,1)$, the pair $T=(X_1,X_2)$ is not complete, because $g(T)=X_1-X_2$ has mean 0 for every $\mu$ but is not almost surely 0.

steps: Start with a [statistic](c:statistic) $T$, a measurable function of the sample that does not depend on $\theta$.
Test every function $g$ of $T$ whose mean $\mathbb{E}_\theta[g(T)]$ is zero for all $\theta$.
Add the condition that each such $g(T)$ is almost surely zero.
Then $T$ is a complete statistic.
links.why: It names the one extra condition that separates a complete statistic from an arbitrary statistic.

reminder: A [consistent theory](c:consistent-theory) is complete when it proves every [sentence](c:sentence) or its negation.
definition: A [consistent theory](c:consistent-theory) $\mathbb{T}$ over a signature $\Sigma$ is complete when, for every [sentence](c:sentence) $\sigma$ over $\Sigma$, either $\mathbb{T}\vdash\sigma$ or $\mathbb{T}\cup\{\sigma\}$ is inconsistent. This says that $\mathbb{T}$ proves $\sigma$ or proves $\neg\sigma$. For a first-order theory, completeness means that all models of $\mathbb{T}$ are [elementarily equivalent](c:elementary-equivalence).
examples: The theory of dense linear orders without endpoints ([DLO](c:dlo)) is complete.
The theory of [algebraically closed fields](c:theory-of-algebraically-closed-fields) of a fixed characteristic is complete.
For any structure $M$, the set of all sentences that are true in $M$ is a complete theory.
Non-example: the theory of groups is not complete, because it proves neither $\forall x\forall y\,(xy=yx)$ nor its negation.

steps: Start with a [consistent theory](c:consistent-theory) $\mathbb{T}$ over a signature $\Sigma$.
Add the condition that for each sentence $\sigma$ over $\Sigma$, $\mathbb{T}$ proves $\sigma$ or proves $\neg\sigma$.
A consistent theory cannot prove both, so exactly one of $\sigma$ and $\neg\sigma$ is provable.
Then $\mathbb{T}$ is a complete theory.
links.why: It shows that a complete theory is a consistent theory that leaves no sentence undecided.

reminder: A rewriting system is confluent when any two reduction paths that start at one element meet again later.
definition: Let $\to$ be the reduction relation of an [abstract rewriting system](c:abstract-rewriting-system), and let $\to^*$ be its reflexive transitive closure. The system is confluent when $a\to^*b$ and $a\to^*c$ imply that some $d$ has $b\to^*d$ and $c\to^*d$. In a confluent system, each element has at most one [normal form](c:normal-form).
examples: On $\mathbb{N}$ let $n\to n-1$ for $n\ge1$. This system is confluent: two reductions from $n$ end at $n-i$ and $n-j$, and the larger one reduces to the smaller one.
Beta reduction in the [lambda calculus](c:lambda-calculus) is confluent. This is the Church–Rosser theorem.
Non-example: take $a\to b$ and $a\to c$ with $b\ne c$ and no other steps. Then $b$ and $c$ never meet, so the system is not confluent.

steps: Let $\to$ be confluent, and let $a\to b$ and $a\to c$ be two single steps.
A single step is a reduction, so $a\to^*b$ and $a\to^*c$.
Confluence gives an element $d$ with $b\to^*d$ and $c\to^*d$.
So $\to$ is [locally confluent](c:locally-confluent-relation), and the converse needs [termination](c:termination).
links.why: It shows that confluence is local confluence with joins of any length, which is why Newman's lemma needs termination.

reminder: The connected component of a point is the largest [connected](c:connected-space) subset of the space that contains it.
definition: Let $X$ be a [topological space](c:topological-space) and $x\in X$. The connected component of $x$ is the union of all [connected](c:connected-space) subsets of $X$ that contain $x$, so it is the largest connected subset that contains $x$. The components of $X$ partition $X$ into closed sets.
examples: In $\mathbb{R}\setminus\{0\}$ the two components are $(-\infty,0)$ and $(0,\infty)$.
In a [connected space](c:connected-space), the whole space is the only component.
In the rational numbers $\mathbb{Q}$, every component is a single point.
Non-example: in $\mathbb{R}\setminus\{0\}$ the set $(-1,0)\cup(0,1)$ is not a component, because it is not connected.

steps: Define $x\sim y$ when some connected subset of $X$ contains both points.
The relation is reflexive and symmetric, because $\{x\}$ is connected and the definition is symmetric.
It is transitive, because two connected sets that share a point have a connected union.
So $\sim$ is an [equivalence relation](c:equivalence-relation), and its [equivalence classes](c:equivalence-class) are the connected components.
links.why: It shows that the components cut the space into disjoint pieces, like the classes of any equivalence relation.

reminder: A language is context-free when a [grammar](c:formal-grammar) whose rules each rewrite a single nonterminal generates it.
definition: A [formal language](c:language) $L$ over an alphabet $\Sigma$ is context-free when a context-free [grammar](c:formal-grammar) generates it. Such a grammar has finitely many rules $A\to w$, where $A$ is one nonterminal and $w$ is a string of terminals and nonterminals, and $L$ is the set of terminal strings that derive from the start symbol. Equivalently, a nondeterministic pushdown automaton accepts $L$.
examples: The language $\{a^nb^n: n\ge0\}$ has the grammar with rules $S\to aSb$ and $S\to\varepsilon$.
The language of balanced brackets, the [Dyck language](c:dyck-language), is context-free.
The palindromes over $\{a,b\}$ are generated by $S\to aSa$, $S\to bSb$, $S\to a$, $S\to b$ and $S\to\varepsilon$.
Non-example: $\{a^nb^nc^n: n\ge0\}$ is not context-free, by the pumping lemma for context-free languages.

steps: Take a [regular language](c:regular-language) and a right-linear grammar that generates it.
Each rule of that grammar has the form $A\to aB$ or $A\to\varepsilon$, so it rewrites one nonterminal.
So the grammar is context-free, and the language is a context-free language.
The converse fails: $\{a^nb^n\}$ is context-free but not regular.
links.why: It shows that context-free languages contain all regular languages and add nested structure such as matching brackets.

steps: Let $G$ be a context-free grammar for $L$ in Chomsky normal form, so each rule is $A\to BC$ or $A\to a$.
A word of length $n\ge1$ then has a derivation of exactly $2n-1$ steps, if it has one.
An algorithm can try all derivations of this length, and there are only finitely many of them.
The algorithm halts on every word and says whether it is in $L$, so $L$ is a [recursive set](c:recursive-subset).
links.why: It shows that membership in a context-free language can always be decided by a program.

reminder: [Random variables](c:random-variable) $X_n$ converge in probability to $X$ when $P(|X_n-X|>\varepsilon)$ tends to 0 for every $\varepsilon>0$.
definition: Let $X_n$ and $X$ be [random variables](c:random-variable) on one probability space. The sequence $X_n$ converges in probability to $X$ when, for every $\varepsilon>0$, the [limit of the sequence](c:limit-of-a-sequence) of numbers $P(|X_n-X|>\varepsilon)$ is 0. We write $X_n\xrightarrow{P}X$.
examples: If $X_n$ is the mean of $n$ independent fair coin tosses, then $X_n$ converges in probability to $1/2$, by the weak law of large numbers.
If $X_n=X+1/n$, then $X_n\to X$ in probability, because $|X_n-X|=1/n$ is below $\varepsilon$ for large $n$.
Non-example: independent fair coin tosses $X_n\in\{0,1\}$ do not converge in probability to $0$, because $P(|X_n|>1/2)=1/2$ for every $n$.

steps: Regard the probability space $(\Omega,\mathcal{F},P)$ as a measure space of total mass 1.
[Convergence in measure](c:convergence-in-measure) says that $\mu(\{|X_n-X|>\varepsilon\})\to0$ for every $\varepsilon>0$.
For $\mu=P$, this is exactly the condition $P(|X_n-X|>\varepsilon)\to0$.
So convergence in probability is convergence in measure for a probability measure.
links.why: It lets a learner use results about convergence in measure for random variables.

steps: Let $X_n\to X$ [almost surely](c:almost-sure-convergence), and fix $\varepsilon>0$.
The events $A_n=\{\sup_{m\ge n}|X_m-X|>\varepsilon\}$ decrease, and their intersection has probability 0.
Continuity of $P$ from above gives $P(A_n)\to0$.
Since $\{|X_n-X|>\varepsilon\}\subseteq A_n$, we get $P(|X_n-X|>\varepsilon)\to0$.
links.why: It shows that almost sure convergence always implies convergence in probability, but not the other way around.

reminder: The $n$-point correlation function of a field is the [expected value](c:expected-value) of the product of the field at $n$ points.
definition: For a random field or [stochastic process](c:stochastic-process) $\phi$, the $n$-point correlation function is $G_n(x_1,\dots,x_n)=\mathbb{E}[\phi(x_1)\cdots\phi(x_n)]$, the [expected value](c:expected-value) of the product of $\phi$ at $n$ points. In quantum field theory, $\mathbb{E}$ is the vacuum expectation value and the product is time ordered. The connected correlation functions come from $G_n$ by subtracting products of lower correlation functions.
examples: For a centered Gaussian field, $G_2(x,y)$ is its covariance, and $G_n=0$ for odd $n$.
For a stationary process $X_t$ with finite variance, the two-point function $\mathbb{E}[X_sX_t]$ depends only on $t-s$.
Non-example: the product $\phi(x)\phi(y)$ is a random variable, not a correlation function; one must take its expected value.

steps: Take a process $X$ with mean $m(x)=\mathbb{E}[X(x)]$ and [covariance function](c:covariance-function) $K(x,y)$.
By definition, the covariance is $K(x,y)=\mathbb{E}[X(x)X(y)]-m(x)m(y)$.
So $K$ is built from the two-point function $G_2$ and the one-point function $G_1=m$.
For a process with mean 0, the covariance function equals $G_2$.
links.why: It shows that the covariance function is the two-point case of the correlation functions.

reminder: The cross product of two vectors in $\mathbb{R}^3$ is the vector perpendicular to both whose length is the area of their parallelogram.
definition: For $u=(u_1,u_2,u_3)$ and $v=(v_1,v_2,v_3)$ in [Euclidean space](c:euclidean-space) $\mathbb{R}^3$, the cross product is $u\times v=(u_2v_3-u_3v_2,\,u_3v_1-u_1v_3,\,u_1v_2-u_2v_1)$. The vector $u\times v$ is [orthogonal](c:orthogonality) to $u$ and to $v$, and its length is $\|u\|\|v\|\sin\theta$ for the angle $\theta$ between them. When $u$ and $v$ are independent, the triple $u,v,u\times v$ is right-handed.
examples: For the standard basis, $e_1\times e_2=e_3$ and $e_2\times e_1=-e_3$.
$(1,2,0)\times(3,1,0)=(0,0,-5)$, which is perpendicular to both factors and has length 5, the area of their parallelogram.
Non-example: the componentwise product $(u_1v_1,u_2v_2,u_3v_3)$ is not the cross product, because in general it is not perpendicular to $u$ and $v$.

steps: Fix $u$; by the formula, each component of $u\times v$ is linear in $v$.
Likewise, for fixed $v$, each component is linear in $u$.
So $\times:\mathbb{R}^3\times\mathbb{R}^3\to\mathbb{R}^3$ is a [bilinear map](c:bilinear-map).
The cross product adds $u\times u=0$, which gives $u\times v=-v\times u$.
links.why: It shows that the cross product is a bilinear map that is also alternating.

reminder: A cut-free proof is a [sequent calculus](c:sequent-calculus) derivation that never uses the [cut rule](c:cut-rule).
definition: In a [sequent calculus](c:sequent-calculus), a [formal proof](c:formal-proof) is a tree of sequents built from axioms by the inference rules. A proof is cut-free when none of its inferences is an instance of the [cut rule](c:cut-rule), which passes from $\Gamma\vdash A,\Delta$ and $\Gamma',A\vdash\Delta'$ to $\Gamma,\Gamma'\vdash\Delta,\Delta'$. In the usual calculi, every formula in a cut-free proof is a subformula of a formula in its conclusion.
examples: The proof of $A\vdash A$ by the identity axiom has no inference, so it is cut-free.
A proof of $A\wedge B\vdash B\wedge A$ that uses only the rules for $\wedge$ is cut-free.
By Gentzen's cut-elimination theorem, each provable sequent of first-order logic has a cut-free proof.
Non-example: a proof that derives $\vdash B$ from $\vdash A$ and $A\vdash B$ by a cut on $A$ is not cut-free.

steps: Take a [formal proof](c:formal-proof) in a sequent calculus, written as a tree of sequents.
Check every inference in the tree.
Add the condition that no inference is an instance of the [cut rule](c:cut-rule).
Then the proof is cut-free.
links.why: It shows that a cut-free proof is an ordinary proof with one rule forbidden.

reminder: A set is decidable when some [Turing machine](c:turing-machine) halts on every input and says whether the input is in the set.
definition: A set $S$ of finite objects, such as the formulas of a [theory](c:theory), is decidable when a [Turing machine](c:turing-machine) halts on every input and answers yes exactly when the input lies in $S$. Any equivalent model of computation, such as the [lambda calculus](c:lambda-calculus), gives the same notion. A theory is decidable when its set of theorems is decidable.
examples: The set of even natural numbers is decidable: divide by 2 and look at the remainder.
The set of theorems of [propositional logic](c:propositional-logic) is decidable, by the method of truth tables.
[Presburger arithmetic](c:presburger-arithmetic), the theory of the natural numbers with addition, is decidable.
Non-example: the halting set $\{(M,x): M \text{ halts on } x\}$ is not decidable, by Turing's theorem.

steps: Let $S$ be decidable, decided by a machine $D$.
List all possible inputs $x_1,x_2,\dots$ one after another.
Run $D$ on each $x_i$, and write $x_i$ in the output list when $D$ says yes.
This procedure lists exactly the members of $S$, so $S$ is [recursively enumerable](c:recursively-enumerable-set).
links.why: It shows that decidable is the stronger condition; the halting set is enumerable but not decidable.

reminder: The derived category of an [abelian category](c:abelian-category) is its [chain complexes](c:chain-complex) with every [quasi-isomorphism](c:quasi-isomorphism) made invertible.
definition: Let $\mathcal{A}$ be an [abelian category](c:abelian-category). Its derived category $D(\mathcal{A})$ has the [chain complexes](c:chain-complex) over $\mathcal{A}$ as objects, and it is the [localization of the category](c:localization-of-a-category) of complexes at the [quasi-isomorphisms](c:quasi-isomorphism), the maps that induce isomorphisms on [homology](c:homology). The category $D(\mathcal{A})$ is a [triangulated category](c:triangulated-category).
examples: For a field $k$, each complex of vector spaces is isomorphic in $D(k\text{-Vect})$ to its homology, so $D(k\text{-Vect})$ is the category of graded vector spaces.
A short exact sequence $0\to A\to B\to C\to0$ gives in $D(\mathcal{A})$ a triangle $A\to B\to C\to A[1]$.
A module $M$ is isomorphic in $D(R\text{-Mod})$ to any projective or injective resolution of $M$, viewed as a complex.
Non-example: the category $\mathrm{Ch}(\mathcal{A})$ of complexes is not the derived category, because a quasi-isomorphism in it need not have an inverse.

steps: Start with the category $\mathrm{Ch}(\mathcal{A})$ of chain complexes and the class $W$ of quasi-isomorphisms.
Form the [localization of the category](c:localization-of-a-category) at $W$, which adds a formal inverse for each map in $W$.
The result has the same objects as $\mathrm{Ch}(\mathcal{A})$, and every quasi-isomorphism becomes an isomorphism.
This localization is the derived category $D(\mathcal{A})$.
links.why: It shows that the derived category is a localization with a known class of maps inverted, so its universal property applies.

reminder: A [square matrix](c:square-matrix) is diagonalizable when it is similar to a [diagonal matrix](c:diagonal-matrix).
definition: A [square matrix](c:square-matrix) $A$ over a field $F$ is diagonalizable when an invertible matrix $P$ exists such that $P^{-1}AP$ is a [diagonal matrix](c:diagonal-matrix). Equivalently, $F^n$ has a [basis](c:basis) that consists of [eigenvectors](c:eigenvector) of $A$.
examples: The matrix $A=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}$ has eigenvectors $(1,1)$ and $(1,-1)$ for the eigenvalues 3 and 1, so it is diagonalizable.
Every real symmetric matrix is diagonalizable, by the spectral theorem.
Every $n\times n$ matrix with $n$ distinct eigenvalues is diagonalizable.
Non-example: $\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$ has only the eigenvectors $(c,0)$, which do not span $\mathbb{R}^2$, so it is not diagonalizable.

steps: Let $D$ be a [diagonal matrix](c:diagonal-matrix).
Take $P=I$, so that $P^{-1}DP=D$ is diagonal.
So $D$ is similar to a diagonal matrix, and $D$ is diagonalizable.
A diagonalizable matrix may need a change of basis first, which a diagonal matrix does not need.
links.why: It shows that diagonalizable matrices are the diagonal matrices up to a change of basis.

reminder: The dimension of a [vector space](c:vector-space) is the number of vectors in any of its [bases](c:basis).
definition: Every [vector space](c:vector-space) $V$ has a [basis](c:basis), and any two bases of $V$ have the same [cardinality](c:cardinal-number). This common cardinality is the dimension $\dim V$. For a finite basis, the dimension is the natural number of its elements.
examples: $\dim\mathbb{R}^n=n$, with the standard basis $e_1,\dots,e_n$.
The polynomials of degree at most $d$ form a space of dimension $d+1$, and $\mathbb{R}[x]$ has infinite dimension with basis $1,x,x^2,\dots$.
Non-example: the spanning set $\{(1,0),(0,1),(1,1)\}$ has three elements, but $\dim\mathbb{R}^2=2$, because this set is not a basis.

reminder: The direct product of a family of algebraic structures is the set of tuples with operations computed in each component.
definition: Let $(A_i)_{i\in I}$ be a family of algebraic structures of one kind, such as [groups](c:group). Their direct product $\prod_{i}A_i$ is the [Cartesian product](c:cartesian-product) of the underlying sets, with each [binary operation](c:binary-operation) defined componentwise, for example $(a_i)_i(b_i)_i=(a_ib_i)_i$. Each projection $\prod_iA_i\to A_j$ is a [homomorphism](c:homomorphism).
examples: The group $\mathbb{Z}/2\times\mathbb{Z}/3$, with $(a,b)+(a',b')=(a+a',b+b')$, is isomorphic to $\mathbb{Z}/6$.
The space $\mathbb{R}^n$ is the direct product of $n$ copies of $\mathbb{R}$, as a vector space and as a ring.
Non-example: $\mathbb{Z}/4$ is not isomorphic to $\mathbb{Z}/2\times\mathbb{Z}/2$, because $\mathbb{Z}/4$ has an element of order 4 and the product has none.

steps: Take groups $G_i$ in the category of groups, with the projections $p_i:\prod G_i\to G_i$.
Let $H$ be a group with homomorphisms $f_i:H\to G_i$.
Define $f(h)=(f_i(h))_i$; it is a homomorphism because the operation of the product is componentwise.
It is the only homomorphism with $p_if=f_i$, so the direct product is a [product](c:product) in the category of groups.
links.why: It shows that the direct product is the categorical product in each category of algebraic structures.

reminder: A Dynkin system is a family of subsets that contains the empty set and is closed under complements and countable disjoint unions.
definition: A Dynkin system on a set $X$ is a family $\mathcal{D}$ of subsets of $X$ with three properties. It contains $\emptyset$, it contains the [complement](c:complement) $X\setminus A$ whenever it contains $A$, and it contains $\bigcup_nA_n$ for each sequence of [pairwise disjoint](c:disjoint-subsets) sets $A_n\in\mathcal{D}$. A Dynkin system that is also a [pi-system](c:pi-system) is a [sigma-algebra](c:sigma-algebra).
examples: On $X=\{1,2,3,4\}$, the family $\{\emptyset,X,\{1,2\},\{3,4\},\{1,3\},\{2,4\}\}$ is a Dynkin system that is not a sigma-algebra.
For two probability measures $P$ and $Q$ on one space, the sets $A$ with $P(A)=Q(A)$ form a Dynkin system.
Non-example: on $X=\{1,2,3\}$, the family $\{\emptyset,\{1\},\{2\},X\}$ is not a Dynkin system, because the complement $\{2,3\}$ of $\{1\}$ is missing.

steps: Let $\mathcal{F}$ be a [sigma-algebra](c:sigma-algebra) on $X$.
It contains $\emptyset$ and is closed under complements.
It is closed under all countable unions, so it is closed under countable disjoint unions.
So $\mathcal{F}$ is a Dynkin system, and the converse needs the extra condition that the system is a [pi-system](c:pi-system).
links.why: It shows that a Dynkin system is a weaker structure than a sigma-algebra, and it explains why the pi-lambda theorem needs a pi-system.

reminder: The eigenspace of a [linear map](c:linear-map) $T$ for a scalar $\lambda$ is the set of all vectors $v$ with $Tv=\lambda v$.
definition: Let $T:V\to V$ be a [linear map](c:linear-map) on a [vector space](c:vector-space) over a field $F$. For $\lambda\in F$, the eigenspace $E_\lambda=\{v\in V: Tv=\lambda v\}$ is the kernel of $T-\lambda I$, so it is a [linear subspace](c:linear-subspace). It holds a nonzero vector exactly when $\lambda$ is an [eigenvalue](c:eigenvalue), and its nonzero elements are the [eigenvectors](c:eigenvector) for $\lambda$.
examples: For $T=\mathrm{diag}(2,2,5)$ on $\mathbb{R}^3$, $E_2$ is the plane spanned by $e_1$ and $e_2$, and $E_5$ is the line spanned by $e_3$.
For the reflection of $\mathbb{R}^2$ in the $x$-axis, $E_1$ is the $x$-axis and $E_{-1}$ is the $y$-axis.
Non-example: for the rotation of $\mathbb{R}^2$ by $90^\circ$, every real eigenspace is $\{0\}$, so there is no real eigenspace that is a line.

steps: Take $v$ in the eigenspace $E_\lambda$, so that $Tv=\lambda v$.
The vector $\lambda v$ lies in $E_\lambda$, because $E_\lambda$ is a subspace.
So $T$ maps $E_\lambda$ into itself, and $E_\lambda$ is an [invariant subspace](c:invariant-subspace).
The eigenspace adds that $T$ acts on it as multiplication by the single scalar $\lambda$.
links.why: It shows that an eigenspace is the simplest invariant subspace, where the map acts as a scalar.

reminder: The Eisenstein series of weight $k$ is a [modular form](c:modular-form) given by the sum of $(c\tau+d)^{-k}$ over coprime pairs $(c,d)$.
definition: For an even integer $k\ge4$ and $\tau$ in the [upper half plane](c:upper-half-plane), let $G_k(\tau)=\sum_{(c,d)\ne(0,0)}(c\tau+d)^{-k}$. This [series](c:series) converges absolutely, and it is a [modular form](c:modular-form) of weight $k$ for $\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb{Z})$. The normalized series $E_k=G_k/(2\zeta(k))$ is half the sum over coprime pairs $(c,d)$, and it has the value 1 at $\tau=i\infty$.
examples: $E_4$ and $E_6$ are modular forms of weights 4 and 6, and every modular form for $\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb{Z})$ is a polynomial in them.
$E_4(\tau)=1+240\sum_{n\ge1}\sigma_3(n)q^n$ with $q=e^{2\pi i\tau}$.
Non-example: for $k=2$ the sum is not absolutely convergent, and the corrected series $E_2$ is not a modular form; it is only quasi-modular.

steps: Fix an even $k\ge4$ and sum $(c\tau+d)^{-k}$ over the nonzero integer pairs $(c,d)$.
The sum converges absolutely and locally uniformly, so it is [holomorphic](c:holomorphic-function) on the upper half plane.
Replacing $\tau$ by $\gamma\tau$ for $\gamma\in\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb{Z})$ permutes the pairs and gives the factor $(c\tau+d)^k$.
The sum stays bounded as $\mathrm{Im}\,\tau\to\infty$, so it is a [modular form](c:modular-form) of weight $k$.
links.why: It shows that Eisenstein series are concrete modular forms that one can write down as a sum.

reminder: Two [structures](c:structure) are elementarily equivalent when they satisfy the same [first-order](c:first-order-logic) sentences.
definition: Let $M$ and $N$ be [structures](c:structure) for one [signature](c:signature-in-logic). They are elementarily equivalent, written $M\equiv N$, when every first-order [sentence](c:sentence) of the signature is true in $M$ exactly when it is true in $N$. Equivalently, $M$ and $N$ have the same complete theory.
examples: $(\mathbb{Q},<)$ and $(\mathbb{R},<)$ are elementarily equivalent, because both are dense linear orders without endpoints, which form a [complete theory](c:complete-theory).
A nonstandard model of the full first-order theory of $(\mathbb{N},+,\cdot)$ is elementarily equivalent to $\mathbb{N}$ but not isomorphic to it.
Non-example: $(\mathbb{Q},<)$ and $(\mathbb{Z},<)$ are not elementarily equivalent, because $\forall x\forall y\,(x<y\to\exists z\,(x<z\wedge z<y))$ is true in $\mathbb{Q}$ and false in $\mathbb{Z}$.

steps: Let $f:M\to N$ be an [elementary embedding](c:elementary-embedding).
For a sentence $\sigma$, which has no parameters, $f$ preserves truth, so $M\models\sigma$ exactly when $N\models\sigma$.
So $M$ and $N$ satisfy the same sentences, and $M\equiv N$.
The converse fails, because $M\equiv N$ gives no map from $M$ to $N$.
links.why: It shows that elementary equivalence forgets the embedding and keeps only the shared first-order truths.

steps: Let $f:M\to N$ be an [isomorphism](c:isomorphism) of structures.
By induction on formulas, $M\models\varphi(\bar a)$ exactly when $N\models\varphi(f\bar a)$.
For a sentence there are no parameters, so $M\models\sigma$ exactly when $N\models\sigma$.
Hence $M\equiv N$, but the converse fails for infinite structures.
links.why: It shows that isomorphic structures cannot be told apart by first-order sentences, although the reverse is false.

reminder: An equivalence relation is a [relation](c:relation) that is reflexive, symmetric and transitive.
definition: A [relation](c:relation) $\sim$ on a set $X$ is an equivalence relation when $x\sim x$ for all $x$, when $x\sim y$ implies $y\sim x$, and when $x\sim y$ and $y\sim z$ imply $x\sim z$. These laws are reflexivity, symmetry and transitivity. The equivalence classes of $\sim$ partition $X$.
examples: Equality on any set is an equivalence relation.
Congruence modulo $n$ on $\mathbb{Z}$, where $a\sim b$ when $n$ divides $a-b$, is an equivalence relation.
Non-example: the order $\le$ on $\mathbb{R}$ is reflexive and transitive but not symmetric, so it is not an equivalence relation.
Non-example: on $\mathbb{R}$, the relation $|a-b|<1$ is reflexive and symmetric but not transitive, because $0\sim0.9$ and $0.9\sim1.8$ but $0\not\sim1.8$.

steps: Start with a [relation](c:relation) $R\subseteq X\times X$.
Add reflexivity: $(x,x)\in R$ for every $x$.
Add symmetry and transitivity.
The result is an equivalence relation, and it splits $X$ into disjoint classes.
links.why: It names the three laws that turn a general relation into a way to identify elements.

reminder: Two [measures](c:measure) are equivalent when they have the same [null sets](c:null-set).
definition:
Let $\mu$ and $
u$ be [measures](c:measure) on one [measurable space](c:measurable-space). They are equivalent, written $\mu\sim
u$, when $\mu(A)=0$ exactly when $
u(A)=0$ for every measurable set $A$. Equivalently, each measure is [absolutely continuous](c:absolutely-continuous-measure) with respect to the other.
examples: Any two Gaussian measures on $\mathbb{R}$ with positive variance are equivalent, because both have the same null sets as Lebesgue measure.
Lebesgue measure and a probability measure with a density $f>0$ everywhere are equivalent.
Non-example: Lebesgue measure on $[0,1]$ and the Dirac measure $\delta_0$ are not equivalent, because $\{0\}$ has Lebesgue measure 0 but $\delta_0(\{0\})=1$.

steps: Take equivalent measures $\mu\sim\nu$ on one space.
If $\nu(A)=0$, then $\mu(A)=0$ by equivalence, so $\mu$ is [absolutely continuous](c:absolutely-continuous-measure) with respect to $\nu$.
The same argument with $\mu$ and $\nu$ swapped shows that $\nu$ is absolutely continuous with respect to $\mu$.
So equivalence adds the second direction to the one-sided relation.
links.why: It shows that equivalent measures are the pairs in which each measure is absolutely continuous with respect to the other.

reminder: An isolated singularity is essential when it is neither removable nor a [pole](c:pole), and its Laurent series has infinitely many negative powers.
definition: Let $f$ be a [holomorphic function](c:holomorphic-function) on a punctured disc around $z_0$, so that $z_0$ is an [isolated singularity](c:isolated-singularity). The singularity is essential when the [Laurent series](c:laurent-series) $\sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}}a_n(z-z_0)^n$ has $a_n\ne0$ for infinitely many $n<0$. Equivalently, $f(z)$ has no limit on the Riemann sphere as $z\to z_0$.
examples: The function $e^{1/z}=\sum_{n\ge0}z^{-n}/n!$ has an essential singularity at $0$.
The function $\sin(1/z)$ has an essential singularity at $0$.
Non-example: $1/z^2$ has a [pole](c:pole) of order 2 at $0$, because its Laurent series has only one negative power.

steps: Let $z_0$ be an [isolated singularity](c:isolated-singularity) of $f$ with Laurent series $\sum a_n(z-z_0)^n$.
If $a_n=0$ for all $n<0$, the singularity is removable.
If $a_n=0$ for all $n<-m$ and $a_{-m}\ne0$, the singularity is a [pole](c:pole) of order $m$.
In the remaining case, infinitely many negative coefficients are nonzero, and the singularity is essential.
links.why: It shows that every isolated singularity is removable, a pole or essential, and essential is the case that remains.

reminder: The functor $\mathrm{Ext}^n_R(M,-)$ is the $n$-th right [derived functor](c:derived-functor) of $\mathrm{Hom}_R(M,-)$.
definition: Let $R$ be a ring and $M$ an $R$-[module](c:module). The functor $\mathrm{Ext}^n_R(M,-)$ is the $n$-th right [derived functor](c:derived-functor) of the left exact [hom-functor](c:hom-functor) $\mathrm{Hom}_R(M,-)$. Concretely, take a resolution $P_\bullet\to M$ by [projective modules](c:projective-module); then $\mathrm{Ext}^n_R(M,N)$ is the $n$-th cohomology of the complex $\mathrm{Hom}_R(P_\bullet,N)$.
examples: $\mathrm{Ext}^0_R(M,N)=\mathrm{Hom}_R(M,N)$ for all modules $M$ and $N$.
$\mathrm{Ext}^1_{\mathbb{Z}}(\mathbb{Z}/n,\mathbb{Z})\cong\mathbb{Z}/n$.
If $M$ is projective, then $\mathrm{Ext}^n_R(M,N)=0$ for all $n\ge1$ and all $N$.
Non-example: the functor $\mathrm{Hom}_R(M,-)$ is only $\mathrm{Ext}^0$; it is not exact in general, and the higher Ext groups measure how far from exact it is.

steps: Fix $M$; then $\mathrm{Hom}_R(M,-)$ is a left exact functor from $R$-modules to abelian groups.
Take an injective resolution $0\to N\to I^0\to I^1\to\cdots$ of $N$.
Apply the functor to $I^\bullet$ and take the $n$-th cohomology of the resulting complex.
This is the $n$-th right [derived functor](c:derived-functor) of $\mathrm{Hom}_R(M,-)$ at $N$, which is $\mathrm{Ext}^n_R(M,N)$.
links.why: It shows that Ext is a derived functor, so the long exact sequence and the resolution methods apply to it.

reminder: A fiber functor is an exact, faithful [functor](c:functor) that sends each object to its underlying finite set or vector space.
definition: A fiber functor is a [functor](c:functor) $F$ out of a [Galois category](c:galois-category) or a [Tannakian category](c:tannakian-category) that records the underlying fiber of each object. In the Galois case, $F:\mathcal{C}\to\mathrm{FinSet}$ preserves finite limits and finite colimits and reflects isomorphisms. In the Tannakian case, $F$ is an exact, faithful tensor functor to vector spaces.
examples: For a finite group $G$, the [forgetful functor](c:forgetful-functor) from finite $G$-sets to finite sets is a fiber functor.
For a connected scheme $X$ with a geometric point $\bar x$, the functor that sends a finite étale cover to its fiber over $\bar x$ is a fiber functor.
The forgetful functor from finite-dimensional representations of a group $G$ to vector spaces is a fiber functor of the Tannakian category $\mathrm{Rep}(G)$.
Non-example: the functor $\mathrm{FinSet}\to\mathrm{FinSet}$ that sends every set to a point is not a fiber functor, because it does not preserve finite coproducts and does not reflect isomorphisms.

steps: Start with a [functor](c:functor) $F:\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{D}$ out of a Galois or Tannakian category $\mathcal{C}$.
Let $\mathcal{D}$ be the category of finite sets or of vector spaces.
Add the conditions that $F$ is exact and that it reflects isomorphisms.
Then $F$ is a fiber functor.
links.why: It names the exactness conditions that turn a plain functor into a tool for Galois and Tannaka theory.

reminder: A fibre bundle is a continuous surjection $p:E\to B$ that looks locally like a projection $U\times F\to U$.
definition: A fibre bundle with fibre $F$ is a continuous [surjection](c:surjection) $p:E\to B$ of [topological spaces](c:topological-space) such that each point of $B$ has an open [neighborhood](c:neighborhood) $U$ and a [homeomorphism](c:homeomorphism) $\varphi:p^{-1}(U)\to U\times F$ with $\mathrm{pr}_1\circ\varphi=p$. Here $U\times F$ has the [product topology](c:product-topology). Such a $\varphi$ is a [local trivialization](c:local-trivialization), and each [fiber](c:fiber) $p^{-1}(b)$ is homeomorphic to $F$.
examples: The Möbius band is a fibre bundle over the circle with fibre an interval, and it is not a product.
The Hopf map $S^3\to S^2$ is a fibre bundle with fibre $S^1$.
Non-example: the projection of the cone $\{x^2+y^2=z^2\}$ to the $z$-axis is not a fibre bundle, because the fibre over $0$ is a point and the other fibres are circles.

steps: Let $p:E\to B$ be a [covering space](c:covering-space) with $B$ connected.
Each point of $B$ has a neighborhood $U$ whose preimage is a disjoint union of copies of $U$.
The index set $F$ of these copies is discrete, and it does not depend on the point because $B$ is connected.
So $p^{-1}(U)\cong U\times F$, and $p$ is a fibre bundle with discrete fibre $F$.
links.why: It shows that a covering space is a fibre bundle whose fibre is a discrete set.

steps: Let $p:E\to B$ be a [vector bundle](c:vector-bundle) of rank $n$ over $\mathbb{R}$.
By definition, every point has a neighborhood $U$ with $p^{-1}(U)\cong U\times\mathbb{R}^n$ over $U$.
This is a local trivialization with fibre $\mathbb{R}^n$.
So the bundle is a fibre bundle, and the vector bundle adds a linear structure on each fibre.
links.why: It shows that a vector bundle is a fibre bundle with fibre $\mathbb{R}^n$ and linear transition maps.

reminder: A first-order theory is a set of axioms written in first-order logic over a fixed [signature](c:signature-in-logic).
definition: A first-order theory consists of a [signature](c:signature-in-logic) and a set of [sentences](c:sentence) of [first-order logic](c:first-order-logic) over it, the axioms. In first-order logic, the quantifiers range over the individual elements of the domain, never over subsets of the domain. The theorems of the theory are the sentences that follow from the axioms.
examples: The theory of groups, with a binary operation, a constant and a unary operation, is a first-order theory.
[Peano arithmetic](c:peano-arithmetic), with an induction schema that has one axiom for each formula, is a first-order theory.
The theory of [dense linear orders](c:dlo) without endpoints is a first-order theory.
Non-example: second-order Peano arithmetic, whose induction axiom quantifies over all subsets of $\mathbb{N}$, is not a first-order theory.

steps: Take a [theory](c:theory): a set of axioms over a signature in some logic.
Choose first-order logic as the logic, so that quantifiers range over elements only.
Then every axiom is a first-order sentence, and the theory is a first-order theory.
links.why: It shows that a first-order theory is a theory with the logic fixed, which gives it completeness and compactness.

reminder: A [module](c:module) $M$ is flat when tensoring with $M$ keeps every injective map injective.
definition: A [module](c:module) $M$ over a ring $R$ is flat when the [tensor product](c:tensor-product) functor $-\otimes_RM$ preserves [injective maps](c:injective-map): if $A\to B$ is injective, then $A\otimes_RM\to B\otimes_RM$ is injective. Equivalently, $-\otimes_RM$ takes every [exact sequence](c:exact-sequence) to an exact sequence.
examples: Every free module is flat, and so is every [projective module](c:projective-module).
$\mathbb{Q}$ is a flat $\mathbb{Z}$-module, because localization preserves injective maps.
Over a field, every module is flat.
Non-example: $\mathbb{Z}/2$ is not a flat $\mathbb{Z}$-module, because tensoring the injection $\mathbb{Z}\xrightarrow{2}\mathbb{Z}$ with $\mathbb{Z}/2$ gives the zero map on $\mathbb{Z}/2$.

steps: Let $P$ be a [projective module](c:projective-module), so that $P\oplus Q$ is a free module for some module $Q$.
Tensoring with a free module is a direct sum of copies of the identity, so it preserves injective maps.
Tensoring with $P\oplus Q$ is tensoring with $P$ and with $Q$ together, so injectivity for the sum gives injectivity for $P$.
So $P$ is flat, and the converse fails: $\mathbb{Q}$ is flat over $\mathbb{Z}$ but not projective.
links.why: It shows that flatness is a weaker condition than projectivity, and it covers modules such as $\mathbb{Q}$.

reminder: A formal group law over a ring is a power series $F(x,y)$ with $F(x,0)=x=F(0,x)$ and $F(x,F(y,z))=F(F(x,y),z)$.
definition: A one-dimensional formal group law over a [commutative ring](c:commutative-ring) $R$ is a [formal power series](c:formal-power-series) $F(x,y)\in R[[x,y]]$ with $F(x,0)=x=F(0,x)$ and $F(x,F(y,z))=F(F(x,y),z)$. It is commutative when $F(x,y)=F(y,x)$. It makes the formal line into a [formal group](c:formal-group).
examples: The additive law $F(x,y)=x+y$.
The multiplicative law $F(x,y)=x+y+xy$, which satisfies $1+F(x,y)=(1+x)(1+y)$.
The expansion of the group law of an elliptic curve in a local parameter at the origin is a formal group law.
Non-example: $F(x,y)=x+y+x^2$ is not a formal group law, because $F(x,0)=x+x^2\ne x$.

steps: Let $F$ be a formal group law over $R$, and let $\mathrm{Spf}\,R[[x]]$ be the formal line.
Define the sum of two points with coordinates $x$ and $y$ to be the point with coordinate $F(x,y)$.
The rule $F(x,0)=x$ gives the unit, and the associativity rule gives the associative law.
Inverses exist as a power series, so this is a [formal group](c:formal-group) with a chosen coordinate.
links.why: It shows that a formal group law is a one-dimensional formal group written in a chosen coordinate.

reminder: A functional equation is an equation between values of an unknown function that characterizes the function.
definition: A functional equation is an [equation](c:equation) whose unknown is a [function](c:function) $f$ and which relates the values of $f$ at different points, such as $f(x+y)=f(x)f(y)$. The equation, often with extra conditions such as continuity, picks out the functions that satisfy it. A solution is a function for which the equation holds for all arguments in the domain.
examples: The Cauchy equation $f(x+y)=f(x)+f(y)$ has the continuous solutions $f(x)=cx$ on $\mathbb{R}$.
The continuous solutions of $f(x+y)=f(x)f(y)$ that are not identically zero are $f(x)=e^{cx}$.
The [Gamma function](c:gamma-function) satisfies $\Gamma(x+1)=x\Gamma(x)$, and with $\Gamma(1)=1$ and log-convexity this equation determines it.
Non-example: $x^2-3x+2=0$ is an equation in a number $x$, not a functional equation, because its unknown is a number and not a function.

reminder: A family of generators of a structure is a family of elements from which all elements arise by the operations.
definition: Let $S$ be an algebraic structure, such as a [group](c:group) or an [algebra](c:algebra) over a ring $R$. A family $(s_i)_{i\in I}$ of elements of $S$ generates $S$ when every element of $S$ comes from the $s_i$ by the operations of $S$; the $s_i$ are then generators. For an $R$-algebra, this means that the algebra map $R[X_i: i\in I]\to S$ with $X_i\mapsto s_i$ is surjective, where $R[X_i: i\in I]$ is a [polynomial ring](c:polynomial-ring).
examples: The integer $1$ generates the group $\mathbb{Z}$ under addition, and so does $-1$.
The variables $x_1,\dots,x_n$ generate the polynomial algebra $R[x_1,\dots,x_n]$ over $R$.
The adjacent transpositions $(i\ \ i+1)$ generate the symmetric group $S_n$.
Non-example: the integer $2$ does not generate $\mathbb{Z}$ under addition, because the odd numbers are not multiples of $2$.

reminder: The genus of a closed orientable [surface](c:surface) counts its handles, and it equals $(2-\chi)/2$ for [Euler characteristic](c:euler-characteristic) $\chi$.
definition: A closed orientable [surface](c:surface) $S$ is homeomorphic to a sphere with $g$ handles attached, and the number $g\ge0$ is the genus of $S$. The genus follows from the [Euler characteristic](c:euler-characteristic) by $\chi(S)=2-2g$, so $g=(2-\chi(S))/2$.
examples: The sphere has genus 0, and the torus has genus 1.
The double torus has genus 2, so its Euler characteristic is $2-4=-2$.
Non-example: the real projective plane has Euler characteristic 1, so the formula would give genus $1/2$; the plane is not orientable and has no genus in this sense.

reminder: A spacetime is globally hyperbolic when it has a [Cauchy surface](c:cauchy-surface) that every inextendible timelike curve meets exactly once.
definition: A connected, time-oriented [Lorentzian manifold](c:lorentzian-manifold) $(M,g)$ is globally hyperbolic when it contains a [Cauchy surface](c:cauchy-surface), a subset that every inextendible timelike curve meets exactly once. Equivalently, $M$ is strongly causal and every causal diamond $J^+(p)\cap J^-(q)$ is compact.
examples: Minkowski space is globally hyperbolic, and the slice $t=0$ is a Cauchy surface.
A product $\mathbb{R}\times\Sigma$ with metric $-dt^2+h$ is globally hyperbolic when $(\Sigma,h)$ is a complete Riemannian manifold.
Non-example: [anti de Sitter spacetime](c:anti-de-sitter-spacetime) is not globally hyperbolic, because light rays reach spatial infinity in finite time, so it has no Cauchy surface.
Non-example: Minkowski space with one point removed is not globally hyperbolic, because some causal diamonds are not compact.

steps: Start with a connected, time-oriented [Lorentzian manifold](c:lorentzian-manifold) $(M,g)$.
Add the condition that $M$ contains a [Cauchy surface](c:cauchy-surface) $S$.
Then every inextendible timelike curve meets $S$ exactly once.
So $M$ is globally hyperbolic, which is the setting where the Cauchy problem for wave equations is well posed.
links.why: It names the one extra condition, a Cauchy surface, that makes initial data determine the whole spacetime.

reminder: An h-cobordism is a [cobordism](c:cobordism) $W$ between manifolds $M$ and $N$ where both inclusions $M\to W$ and $N\to W$ are [homotopy equivalences](c:homotopy-equivalence).
definition: An h-cobordism is a [cobordism](c:cobordism) $(W;M,N)$ between closed [manifolds](c:manifold) $M$ and $N$, so that $\partial W=M\sqcup N$. It is an h-cobordism when each inclusion $M\hookrightarrow W$ and $N\hookrightarrow W$ is a [homotopy equivalence](c:homotopy-equivalence). Then $M$ and $N$ are homotopy equivalent.
examples: The product $M\times[0,1]$ is an h-cobordism between $M\times\{0\}$ and $M\times\{1\}$.
By Smale's h-cobordism theorem, a simply connected h-cobordism of dimension at least 6 is a product $M\times[0,1]$.
Non-example: the disc $D^2$ is a cobordism from the empty manifold to $S^1$, but the inclusion of $\emptyset$ into $D^2$ is not a homotopy equivalence, so $D^2$ is not an h-cobordism.

steps: Start with a [cobordism](c:cobordism) $W$ with $\partial W=M\sqcup N$.
Add the condition that the inclusion $M\hookrightarrow W$ is a [homotopy equivalence](c:homotopy-equivalence).
Add the same condition for the inclusion $N\hookrightarrow W$.
Then $W$ is an h-cobordism, and $M$ and $N$ have the same homotopy type.
links.why: It names the two homotopy conditions that separate an h-cobordism from a general cobordism.

reminder: The Hardy space $H^p$ holds the [holomorphic functions](c:holomorphic-function) on the unit disc whose $L^p$ means on circles stay bounded.
definition: For $0<p<\infty$, the Hardy space $H^p$ is the set of [holomorphic functions](c:holomorphic-function) $f$ on the [unit disc](c:unit-disc) with $\sup_{0<r<1}\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}|f(re^{i\theta})|^p\,d\theta<\infty$. The space $H^\infty$ holds the bounded holomorphic functions. For $p\ge1$, each $f\in H^p$ has boundary values on the circle, and $H^p$ is a closed subspace of the [Lp space](c:lp-space) of the circle.
examples: Every bounded holomorphic function on the disc, such as a polynomial, lies in $H^p$ for every $p$.
The function $(1-z)^{-a}$ with $a>0$ lies in $H^p$ exactly when $ap<1$.
Non-example: $f(z)=1/(1-z)$ is holomorphic on the disc but lies in no $H^p$ with $p\ge1$, because the integrals of $|f|^p$ over the circles of radius $r$ blow up as $r\to1$.

reminder: A Hermitian form on a [complex vector space](c:complex-vector-space) is linear in one argument and conjugate-linear in the other, with $h(w,v)=\overline{h(v,w)}$.
definition: A Hermitian form on a [complex vector space](c:complex-vector-space) $V$ is a [sesquilinear form](c:sesquilinear-form) $h:V\times V\to\mathbb{C}$, linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the second, with $h(w,v)=\overline{h(v,w)}$. Here the bar is [complex conjugation](c:complex-conjugation). In particular, $h(v,v)$ is a real number for every $v$.
examples: On $\mathbb{C}^n$, the form $h(z,w)=\sum_iz_i\overline{w_i}$ is a Hermitian form.
For a matrix $A$ with $A^*=A$, the form $h(z,w)=w^*Az$ is a Hermitian form on $\mathbb{C}^n$.
Non-example: $b(z,w)=zw$ on $\mathbb{C}$ is not Hermitian, because it is linear in $w$, and a Hermitian form must be conjugate-linear in $w$.

steps: Start with a [sesquilinear form](c:sesquilinear-form) $h$ on $V$, linear in the first and conjugate-linear in the second argument.
Add the condition $h(w,v)=\overline{h(v,w)}$ for all $v$ and $w$.
Then $h(v,v)=\overline{h(v,v)}$, so $h(v,v)$ is real for every $v$.
Such an $h$ is a Hermitian form.
links.why: It names the one extra condition, conjugate symmetry, that makes the values $h(v,v)$ real.

steps: Let $V$ be a complex [inner product space](c:inner-product-space) with inner product $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle$.
The inner product is linear in one argument, conjugate-linear in the other, and conjugate symmetric.
So it is a Hermitian form.
An inner product adds positive definiteness: $\langle v,v\rangle>0$ for every $v\ne0$.
links.why: It shows that an inner product is a Hermitian form that is also positive definite.

reminder: An HNN extension adds to a [group](c:group) $G$ a new element $t$ that conjugates one subgroup onto another by a given [isomorphism](c:isomorphism).
definition: Let $G$ be a [group](c:group), let $A,B\le G$ be [subgroups](c:subgroup), and let $\varphi:A\to B$ be an [isomorphism](c:isomorphism). The HNN extension is the group $G*_\varphi=\langle G,t\mid tat^{-1}=\varphi(a)\text{ for all }a\in A\rangle$, which adds one new generator $t$ and these relations. The map $G\to G*_\varphi$ is injective (Higman, Neumann and Neumann), so $G$ is a subgroup of $G*_\varphi$ in which $t$ conjugates $A$ onto $B$.
examples: With $G=\{1\}$, the HNN extension is the infinite cyclic group $\langle t\rangle\cong\mathbb{Z}$.
With $G=\langle a\rangle\cong\mathbb{Z}$, $A=B=G$ and $\varphi(a)=a^{-1}$, the HNN extension is $\langle a,t\mid tat^{-1}=a^{-1}\rangle$, the fundamental group of the Klein bottle.
The Baumslag–Solitar group $\langle a,t\mid ta^mt^{-1}=a^n\rangle$ is the HNN extension of $\mathbb{Z}=\langle a\rangle$ with $A=\langle a^m\rangle$, $B=\langle a^n\rangle$ and $\varphi(a^m)=a^n$.
Non-example: for $G=\mathbb{Z}$ with $A=G$ and $B=\{1\}$ there is no isomorphism $A\to B$, and the relation $tat^{-1}=1$ would kill $a$, so $G$ would not embed.

reminder: Real numbers $p,q>1$ are Hölder conjugate exponents when $1/p+1/q=1$.
definition: Two [real numbers](c:real-number) $p,q>1$ are Hölder conjugate exponents when $\frac1p+\frac1q=1$, which means that $q=p/(p-1)$. Some texts also allow the pair $(1,\infty)$. These exponents appear in Hölder's inequality $\|fg\|_1\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_q$.
examples: The exponents $p=q=2$ are conjugate, and Hölder's inequality becomes the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality.
The exponents $p=3$ and $q=3/2$ are conjugate, because $1/3+2/3=1$.
Non-example: $p=q=3$ are not conjugate, because $1/3+1/3=2/3\ne1$.

steps: A [Hölder triple](c:holder-triple) is a triple $(p,q,r)$ of exponents with $1/p+1/q=1/r$.
Set $r=1$ to get the condition $1/p+1/q=1$.
So a pair of conjugate exponents is the same as a Hölder triple $(p,q,1)$.
Hölder's inequality for a triple then reduces to $\|fg\|_1\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_q$.
links.why: It shows that conjugate exponents are the case $r=1$ of the general Hölder condition.

reminder: The index of a [subgroup](c:subgroup) $H$ in a group $G$ is the number of left [cosets](c:coset) of $H$ in $G$.
definition: For a [subgroup](c:subgroup) $H\le G$, the index $[G:H]$ is the [cardinality](c:cardinal-number) of the set $G/H$ of left [cosets](c:coset) $gH$. This is also the number of right cosets. If $G$ is finite, Lagrange's theorem gives $[G:H]=|G|/|H|$.
examples: $[\mathbb{Z}:n\mathbb{Z}]=n$ for every $n\ge1$.
$[S_n:A_n]=2$ for $n\ge2$.
Non-example: the index is not the order of $H$; in $S_3$ the subgroup $A_3$ has order 3 but index 2.

steps: Take a group $G$ and the trivial subgroup $H=\{e\}$.
Each left coset $gH=\{g\}$ is a single element.
So the cosets match the elements of $G$ one to one.
Hence $[G:\{e\}]=|G|$, the [order of the group](c:order-of-a-group) $G$.
links.why: It shows that the order of a group is the index of its trivial subgroup.

reminder: A set is infinite when it is not in [bijection](c:bijection) with $\{1,\dots,n\}$ for any natural number $n$.
definition: A [set](c:set) $X$ is infinite when it is not [finite](c:finite-set), that is, when there is no natural number $n$ and no [bijection](c:bijection) between $X$ and $\{1,\dots,n\}$. For every $n$, an infinite set has a subset with exactly $n$ elements.
examples: The set $\mathbb{N}$ of natural numbers is infinite.
The open interval $(0,1)$ is infinite, and so is $\mathbb{R}$.
Non-example: the set of letters of the English alphabet is finite, because it is in bijection with $\{1,\dots,26\}$.

reminder: An initial object of a [category](c:category) has exactly one morphism to each object of the category.
definition: An object $I$ of a [category](c:category) $\mathcal{C}$ is initial when, for every object $X$ of $\mathcal{C}$, there is exactly one morphism $I\to X$. Any two initial objects are [isomorphic](c:isomorphism) by a unique isomorphism. An initial object is the [colimit](c:colimit) of the empty diagram.
examples: The empty set is initial in the category of sets, because there is exactly one function from $\emptyset$ to any set.
The trivial group is initial in the category of groups, and it is also terminal.
The ring $\mathbb{Z}$ is initial in the category of rings with unit.
Non-example: a one-point set is not initial in the category of sets, because there are several functions from it to a set with two elements.

steps: Take the empty diagram in $\mathcal{C}$, with no objects and no arrows.
A cocone under the empty diagram is just an object $X$ of $\mathcal{C}$.
A [colimit](c:colimit) has a unique map to every cocone, so here it is an object $I$ with a unique map to each $X$.
This is exactly an initial object, so an initial object is the colimit of the empty diagram.
links.why: It shows that initial objects are colimits, so results about colimits cover them.

reminder: A ring extension $A\subseteq B$ is integral when every element of $B$ is a root of a monic polynomial over $A$.
definition: Let $A\subseteq B$ be a [ring extension](c:ring-extension) of [commutative rings](c:commutative-ring). An element $b\in B$ is integral over $A$ when $f(b)=0$ for some monic [polynomial](c:polynomial) $f\in A[x]$. The extension is integral when every element of $B$ is integral over $A$.
examples: $\mathbb{Z}\subseteq\mathbb{Z}[i]$ is integral, because $a+bi$ is a root of the monic polynomial $x^2-2ax+a^2+b^2$.
If $B$ is a finitely generated $A$-module, then $A\subseteq B$ is integral.
Non-example: $\mathbb{Z}\subseteq\mathbb{Q}$ is not integral, because $1/2$ is a root of no monic polynomial over $\mathbb{Z}$.

steps: Let $K\subseteq L$ be an [algebraic extension](c:algebraic-extension) of fields, and let $\alpha\in L$.
Then $\alpha$ is a root of a nonzero polynomial $f$ over $K$.
Divide $f$ by its leading coefficient, which is a unit of $K$, to get a monic polynomial with root $\alpha$.
So every $\alpha\in L$ is integral over $K$, and $K\subseteq L$ is an integral extension.
links.why: It shows that integrality is algebraicity for rings that are not fields.

reminder: A [morphism of schemes](c:morphism-of-schemes) is proper when it is [separated](c:is-separated), [universally closed](c:universally-closed) and [locally of finite type](c:locally-of-finite-type).
definition: A [morphism of schemes](c:morphism-of-schemes) $f:X\to Y$ is proper when it is [separated](c:is-separated), [universally closed](c:universally-closed) and [locally of finite type](c:locally-of-finite-type). Universally closed means that every base change of $f$ is a [closed map](c:closed-map) of the underlying spaces. Proper morphisms are the algebraic version of maps with compact fibres.
examples: The structure morphism $\mathbb{P}^n_k\to\mathrm{Spec}\,k$ of projective space is proper.
A finite morphism, such as $\mathrm{Spec}\,B\to\mathrm{Spec}\,A$ for a finite $A$-algebra $B$, is proper.

Non-example: $\mathbb{A}^1_k\to\mathrm{Spec}\,k$ is not proper, because its base change $\mathbb{A}^2\to\mathbb{A}^1$ sends the closed curve $xy=1$ onto $\mathbb{A}^1\setminus\{0\}$, which is not closed.

steps: Let $i:Z\to Y$ be a [closed immersion](c:is-closed-immersion).
It is separated, because a closed immersion is a monomorphism and so its diagonal is an isomorphism.
It is universally closed, because closed immersions are closed maps and stay closed immersions under base change.
It is locally of finite type, because locally it is $\mathrm{Spec}\,A/I\to\mathrm{Spec}\,A$, so $i$ is proper.
links.why: It shows that every closed immersion is proper, so closed subschemes of proper schemes are proper.

reminder: The Jacobian of a smooth projective curve is an [abelian variety](c:abelian-variety) whose points are the degree-zero [divisor](c:divisor) classes.
definition: Let $C$ be a smooth projective [algebraic curve](c:algebraic-curve) of genus $g$ over a field. Its Jacobian $J(C)$ is the [abelian variety](c:abelian-variety) of dimension $g$ whose points are the [divisors](c:divisor) of degree 0 on $C$ modulo linear equivalence. Over $\mathbb{C}$, $J(C)=H^0(C,\Omega^1)^\vee/H_1(C,\mathbb{Z})$, a complex torus.
examples: For a curve of genus 0, the Jacobian is a point.
For an elliptic curve $E$ with origin $O$, the Jacobian $J(E)$ is isomorphic to $E$ by $P\mapsto[P-O]$.
Non-example: for $g\ge2$ the curve $C$ is not its own Jacobian, because $C$ has dimension 1 and $J(C)$ has dimension $g$.

steps: Let $C$ be a smooth projective curve of genus $g$.
Its degree-zero divisor classes form a group, the group of points of $\mathrm{Pic}^0(C)$.
This group is the set of points of a smooth projective connected group variety of dimension $g$.
A complete connected group variety is an [abelian variety](c:abelian-variety), so $J(C)$ is one.
links.why: It shows that the Jacobian is an abelian variety that comes from a curve, so the theory of abelian varieties applies to it.

steps: The [Picard scheme](c:picard-scheme) $\mathrm{Pic}_C$ parametrizes line bundles on $C$, and so divisor classes.
Taking the degree of a divisor class gives a map $\mathrm{Pic}_C\to\mathbb{Z}$.
The fibre over $0$ is the subscheme $\mathrm{Pic}^0_C$ of degree-zero classes.
For a smooth projective curve, $\mathrm{Pic}^0_C$ is the Jacobian, the identity component of $\mathrm{Pic}_C$.
links.why: It shows that the Jacobian is the degree-zero part of the Picard scheme of the curve.

reminder: The $k$-th jet bundle of a [fibre bundle](c:fibre-bundle) $E\to X$ records the Taylor data up to order $k$ of local sections.
definition: Let $\pi:E\to X$ be a [fibre bundle](c:fibre-bundle) of [smooth manifolds](c:smooth-manifold). Two local sections of $\pi$ have the same $k$-jet at $x\in X$ when their [Taylor series](c:taylor-series) at $x$ agree up to order $k$ in local coordinates. The $k$-th jet bundle $J^kE$ is the set of all $k$-jets of local sections, and it is a smooth fibre bundle over $X$.
examples: $J^0E=E$, because a $0$-jet at $x$ is the value of a section at $x$.
For $E=\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$, the jet bundle $J^2E$ has coordinates $(x,u,u',u'')$, and a second order ordinary differential equation is a subset of it.
Non-example: the infinite sequence of all derivatives at a point is an infinite jet, not a point of $J^kE$ for any finite $k$.

steps: Take a chart $U\subseteq X$ over which $E$ is trivial, with coordinates $(x^i,u^a)$.
A $k$-jet of a section at a point of $U$ is given by the values of $u^a$ and their partial derivatives up to order $k$.
So $J^kE$ over $U$ is identified with $U\times\mathbb{R}^N$ for a fixed number $N$.
These identifications are local trivializations, so $J^kE\to X$ is a [fibre bundle](c:fibre-bundle).
links.why: It shows that the jet bundle is a fibre bundle, so the tools for bundles apply to it.

reminder: The kernel of a [homomorphism](c:homomorphism) is the set of elements that it maps to the identity element.
definition: For a [group homomorphism](c:group-homomorphism) $f:G\to H$, the kernel is $\ker f=\{g\in G: f(g)=e_H\}$, the preimage of the [identity element](c:identity-element). For a linear map or a ring homomorphism, the kernel is the preimage of $0$. The kernel is a [normal subgroup](c:normal-subgroup), and $f$ is injective exactly when $\ker f$ is trivial.
examples: The kernel of the determinant $\det:\mathrm{GL}_n(\mathbb{R})\to\mathbb{R}^\times$ is $\mathrm{SL}_n(\mathbb{R})$.
The kernel of the reduction map $\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{Z}/n$ is $n\mathbb{Z}$.
The kernel of the sign map $S_n\to\{\pm1\}$ is the alternating group $A_n$.
Non-example: the set of elements $g$ with $f(g)\ne e$ is not the kernel, and it is not a subgroup, because it does not contain $e$.

steps: Let $K=\ker f$, and take $k\in K$ and $g\in G$.
Then $f$ maps $gkg^{-1}$ to $f(g)f(k)f(g)^{-1}=f(g)f(g)^{-1}=e$.
So $gkg^{-1}\in K$, and $K$ is a [normal subgroup](c:normal-subgroup).
Conversely, each normal subgroup $N$ is the kernel of the quotient map $G\to G/N$.
links.why: It shows that kernels of homomorphisms and normal subgroups are the same subgroups.

steps: Let $f:G\to H$ be a group homomorphism, and let $0:G\to H$ be the trivial homomorphism $g\mapsto e$.
The [equalizer](c:equalizer) of $f$ and $0$ is the subgroup $\{g: f(g)=0(g)\}$ with its inclusion into $G$.
This subgroup is $\{g: f(g)=e\}=\ker f$.
So the kernel is the equalizer of $f$ and the trivial map, taken in the category of groups.
links.why: It shows that the kernel is an equalizer, which explains why it exists in every category of this kind.

reminder: A family of measures obeys a large deviation principle when rare-event probabilities decay exponentially at a rate given by a [rate function](c:rate-function).
definition: Let $(\mu_\varepsilon)_{\varepsilon>0}$ be a family of [probability measures](c:probability-measure) on a topological space $X$, and let $I:X\to[0,\infty]$ be a [lower semicontinuous](c:lower-semicontinuous-function) function, the [rate function](c:rate-function). The family satisfies a large deviation principle with rate function $I$ when $\limsup_{\varepsilon\to0}\varepsilon\log\mu_\varepsilon(F)\le-\inf_FI$ for every [closed set](c:closed-set) $F$ and $\liminf_{\varepsilon\to0}\varepsilon\log\mu_\varepsilon(G)\ge-\inf_GI$ for every [open set](c:open-set) $G$.
examples: For the sample mean of independent identically distributed real variables with finite exponential moments, Cramér's theorem gives a large deviation principle at $\varepsilon=1/n$, with the Legendre transform of the log moment generating function as rate function.
The scaled Brownian paths $\sqrt{\varepsilon}\,B$ satisfy a large deviation principle on path space with rate $\frac12\int_0^1|\dot\omega|^2\,dt$, by Schilder's theorem.

Non-example: let $\mu_n=\delta_0$ for even $n$ and $\mu_n=\delta_1$ for odd $n$, with $\varepsilon=1/n$. The upper bound for the closed set $\{0\}$ forces $I(0)=0$, but the open set $(-\tfrac12,\tfrac12)$ has $\mu_n=0$ for odd $n$, so the lower bound fails.

reminder: A family of subsets of a [topological space](c:topological-space) is locally finite when every point has a [neighborhood](c:neighborhood) that meets only finitely many members.
definition: Let $(A_i)_{i\in I}$ be a family of subsets of a [topological space](c:topological-space) $X$. The family is locally finite when every point $x\in X$ has a [neighborhood](c:neighborhood) $U$ such that $\{i\in I: U\cap A_i\ne\emptyset\}$ is finite. Every finite family is locally finite, and the closures of the members of a locally finite family again form a locally finite family.
examples: The intervals $[n,n+1]$ for $n\in\mathbb{Z}$ form a locally finite family in $\mathbb{R}$.
Every finite family of subsets is locally finite.
Non-example: the intervals $[1/(n+1),1/n]$ for $n\ge1$ are not locally finite in $\mathbb{R}$, because every neighborhood of $0$ meets infinitely many of them.

steps: Let $\mathcal{U}$ be a [locally finite cover](c:locally-finite-cover) of $X$.
By definition, every point has a neighborhood that meets only finitely many sets of $\mathcal{U}$.
So $\mathcal{U}$, viewed as a family of subsets, is a locally finite family.
A locally finite family needs no covering condition, so it may leave part of $X$ uncovered.
links.why: It shows that local finiteness is a property of a family of sets, whether or not the family covers the space.

reminder: The Lorentz group is the group of linear maps of [Minkowski space](c:minkowski-space) that preserve the [quadratic form](c:quadratic-form) $t^2-x^2-y^2-z^2$.
definition: The Lorentz group is $O(1,3)=\{\Lambda\in\mathrm{GL}_4(\mathbb{R}):\Lambda^T\eta\Lambda=\eta\}$ with $\eta=\mathrm{diag}(1,-1,-1,-1)$, the linear maps of [Minkowski space](c:minkowski-space) that preserve the [quadratic form](c:quadratic-form) $t^2-x^2-y^2-z^2$. It is a [Lie group](c:lie-group) of dimension 6 with four connected components. Its identity component is the proper orthochronous Lorentz group $SO^+(1,3)$.
examples: A rotation of the spatial coordinates $(x,y,z)$ with $t$ fixed belongs to the Lorentz group.
A boost along the $x$-axis, $t'=\gamma(t-vx)$ and $x'=\gamma(x-vt)$ with $\gamma=(1-v^2)^{-1/2}$, belongs to the Lorentz group, because $t'^2-x'^2=t^2-x^2$.
Non-example: a translation $x\mapsto x+a$ with $a\ne0$ is not linear, so it is not in the Lorentz group; it lies in the [Poincaré group](c:poincare-group).

steps: The [orthogonal group](c:orthogonal-group) of a quadratic form $Q$ is the group of linear maps $\Lambda$ with $Q(\Lambda v)=Q(v)$.
Choose $Q=t^2-x^2-y^2-z^2$ on $\mathbb{R}^4$, which has signature $(1,3)$.
The orthogonal group of this form is $O(1,3)$.
So the Lorentz group is the orthogonal group of the Minkowski quadratic form.
links.why: It shows that the Lorentz group is the orthogonal group for a form that is not positive definite.

steps: The condition $\Lambda^T\eta\Lambda=\eta$ is a set of polynomial equations in the entries of $\Lambda$.
So $O(1,3)$ is a closed subgroup of the matrix group $\mathrm{GL}_4(\mathbb{R})$.
By the closed subgroup theorem, a closed subgroup of a [Lie group](c:lie-group) is a Lie group.
So the Lorentz group is a Lie group of dimension 6.
links.why: It shows that the Lorentz group has a Lie algebra, and so one can study it by infinitesimal methods.

reminder: A monoid is a set with an associative [binary operation](c:binary-operation) and an [identity element](c:identity-element).
definition: A monoid is a [set](c:set) $M$ with a [binary operation](c:binary-operation) $\cdot:M\times M\to M$ and an [identity element](c:identity-element) $e\in M$ such that $(a\cdot b)\cdot c=a\cdot(b\cdot c)$ and $e\cdot a=a=a\cdot e$ for all $a,b,c\in M$. It is commutative when $a\cdot b=b\cdot a$ for all $a,b$.
examples: The natural numbers $\mathbb{N}$ with addition and the identity $0$ form a monoid.
The strings over an alphabet, with concatenation and the empty string as identity, form a monoid.
The functions $X\to X$ on a set $X$, with composition and the identity map, form a monoid.
Non-example: $(\mathbb{Z},-)$ is not a monoid, because the operation is not associative: $(3-2)-1=0$ but $3-(2-1)=2$.

steps: Start with a [semigroup](c:semigroup): a set with an associative binary operation.
Add an element $e$ with $e\cdot a=a=a\cdot e$ for every $a$.
The result is a monoid, and forgetting $e$ turns a monoid back into a semigroup.
links.why: It shows that a monoid is a semigroup with a chosen identity element.

steps: Let $G$ be a [group](c:group) with operation $\cdot$ and identity $e$.
The operation is associative and $e$ is an identity element, by the group axioms.
So $(G,\cdot,e)$ is a monoid, once we forget the inverses.
A monoid is a group exactly when every element has an inverse.
links.why: It shows that a group is a monoid in which every element has an inverse.
